creator: pre_placement_preparations
caption: A customer asks Al to summarize an email.  Another uploads a financial report.  A third needs help solving a complex business problem.  Should all three requests use the same Al model?  Probably not.  And this is one of the most important decisions in Enterprise Al architecture.  Choosing the right model affects cost, latency, accuracy, and infrastructure requirements.  Let's look at 4 types of Al models and where they fit.  1. Large Language Models (LLMS)  Designed for general-purpose tasks that require broad knowledge and language understanding.  Best for: Enterprise copilots, content generation, summarization, and RAG applications.  Examples: GPT, Claude, Gemini, Mistral Large.  2. Small Language Models (SLMS)  Compact models optimized for efficiency, lower costs, and specialized tasks.  Best for: Classification, information extraction, high-volume automation, and on-device Al.  Examples: Phi, Gemma, Llama 3.2 3B, Mistral 7B.  3. Large Reasoning Models (LRMS)  Models that use additional inference-time computation to handle complex problems.  Best for: Multi-step analysis, mathematical reasoning, coding, and planning.  Examples: OpenAl o-series, DeepSeek-R1, reasoning modes in Claude and Gemini.  4. Vision Language Models (VLMS)  Models capable of understanding visual information alongside text.  Best for: Document processing, invoice extraction, screenshots, charts, and image analysis.  Examples: GPT-40, Gemini, Qwen-VL, LLaVA.  Now, here's where enterprise architecture gets interesting.  Instead of sending every request to one expensive model, introduce intelligent model routing.  Simple, repetitive task? Use an SLM.  Complex reasoning required? Route to an LRM.  Image or scanned document? Choose a VLM.  Broad, open-ended question? Use an LLM.  These categories can overlap, so evaluate models against your actual workloads.  The goal is to balance quality, speed, cost, and security.  Because the future of Enterprise Al isn't about deploying one powerful model everywhere. . . Follow for more 👉  @pre_placement_preparations . . #ai #coder #programming #softwaredeveloper #developer

creator: 0x.gaurav
caption: The newest way to code with AI is an idea from 1970.  If you build with ChatGPT or Cursor, you know the loop: “make it work”, regenerate, 1:57 AM. Every detail you didn’t write down, the AI decided for you. The AI-era name for writing it down first is spec-driven development. A spec (short for specification) is a short note of exactly what you want; the AI builds from it and tests against it.  The idea is old. In 1970, W.W. Royce drew the step-by-step staircase that later got called “waterfall”, and wrote right under it that the approach “is risky and invites failure”. GitHub’s open-source Spec Kit is one 2025 take on it: 144,070 stars (30 Oct 2026).  What’s one thing your AI decided for you that you only noticed later?  Sources: W.W. Royce, “Managing the Development of Large Software Systems”, Proc. IEEE WESCON, Aug 1970 · A. creator: philosophyofphys
caption: The holographic principle is one of the alternative ways of understanding the universe we live in. It proposes that the physics inside a region of space can be fully described by degrees of freedom on its boundary, one dimension lower.  The idea starts with black hole entropy. Bekenstein and Hawking showed that a black hole has entropy  S = A / 4ℓₚ²  where A is the area of the event horizon and ℓₚ² = Għ/c³ is the Planck area, about 2.6 × 10⁻⁷⁰ m². The entropy scales with area, not volume. That is unusual. In ordinary quantum field theory, the number of degrees of freedom in a region grows with its volume.  The black hole result turns out to be a universal limit. Suppose a region contains more entropy than a black hole of the same size. Add a little mass and it collapses into a black hole, whose entropy is only A/4ℓₚ². Entropy would then have decreased, violating the second law. So the maximum entropy any region can hold is set by its boundary area. This means the true number of degrees of freedom in nature scales like area. A volume-based description overcounts.  From this, 't Hooft (1993) and Susskind (1995) proposed that a theory of quantum gravity in a region should be equivalent to a theory living on its boundary. In 1997, Maldacena made this precise with the AdS/CFT correspondence: string theory in five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space is exactly equivalent to a four-dimensional quantum field theory without gravity on its boundary. Later, the Ryu–Takayanagi formula showed that the entanglement entropy of a boundary region equals the area of a minimal surface in the bulk, divided by 4G. Bulk geometry is encoded in boundary entanglement.  There are clear limits. AdS/CFT works for negatively curved spacetime, but our universe, dominated by dark energy, is close to de Sitter, with positive curvature. Bousso's covariant entropy bound extends the area law to general spacetimes, but no complete holographic description of our universe exists, and there is no direct experimental test yet.

creator: ml.with.umang
caption: Math for ML is simpler than it looks.  You do not need to master every branch of mathematics to become a strong ML Engineer. You need to understand the areas that repeatedly show up in models, training, evaluation, and system behavior.  The core stack looks like this:  → Linear Algebra: vectors, matrices, dot products, eigenvalues, SVD → Probability: conditional probability, Bayes’ theorem, expectation, variance → Statistics: distributions, confidence intervals, covariance, correlation → Multivariable Calculus: gradients, Jacobians, Hessians, backpropagation → Optimization: loss functions, gradient descent, Adam, learning rates → Information Theory: entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence → Distance & Similarity: Euclidean, Manhattan, cosine similarity, vector search → Statistical Learning: bias-variance, regularization, MLE, MAP → Numerical Computing: stability, normalization, mixed precision  What matters most is knowing where each concept appears.  Cosine similarity shows up in embeddings and retrieval. Cross-entropy appears in classification. Gradients power backpropagation. SVD helps with dimensionality reduction. Bias-variance explains underfitting and overfitting.  That is the mindset I recommend for learning ML math.  Study concepts through models, implementations, and systems you actually build.  Once you do that, the math becomes easier to remember and much more useful in interviews and real ML engineering work.  #usa #tech #ai #ml

caption: I’m developing a taxonomy of visuals that connects images through the techniques and ideas behind them.  I think we all want to understand the thinking behind the references we collect, and how we can apply those ideas to our own work. How can we give an image more meaning? How can we translate an idea into a visual?  None of this is entirely new. The principles and techniques themselves have been taught for decades. There are creatives, designers, and art directors who are masters at it. But so much of that knowledge is instinctual. Visually mapping the mechanisms behind an image’s style and aesthetic, and connecting those techniques to what it communicates, is the part I’m developing. That’s the part that I haven’t seen anyone do in this specific way.  And it feels especially valuable now, when we’re inundated with imagery. Understanding why visuals work helps us make deliberate choices, explain our thinking, and direct the work as the tools and possibilities keep changing. caption: What if the universe is just one giant simulation? 🌌💻  Everything around us—from the motion of planets to the behavior of particles—follows mathematical laws. But what happens when we translate those laws into computer code?  That’s where Numerical Recipes in C++: The Art of Scientific Computing comes in.  Written by William H. Press, Saul A. Teukolsky, William T. Vetterling, and Brian P. Flannery, this legendary book explores how mathematics, physics, and computer programming come together to solve complex scientific problems.  🔹 Numerical Methods: How do computers solve mathematical equations that are difficult or impossible to solve analytically?  🔹 Computational Physics: Can we simulate gravity, planetary motion, fluid dynamics, and physical systems using C++?  🔹 Linear Algebra: How do matrices, vectors, and numerical algorithms help us model the physical world?  🔹 Differential Equations: How can we predict the motion of objects, the flow of fluids, or the evolution of physical systems?  🔹 Scientific Computing: How do scientists use algorithms, numerical integration, optimization, and computational mathematics to understand reality?  The fascinating part?  Many of the equations describing our universe can be approximated and simulated using relatively simple algorithms.  From Newton’s laws of motion to quantum mechanics, chaos theory, and astrophysics, mathematical models allow us to recreate aspects of the physical world inside a computer.  Does that prove we’re living in a simulation? No. But it raises an interesting question:  If we can simulate the laws of physics using mathematics and code, how far could those simulations go?  This is what makes the intersection of mathematics, C++ programming, computational physics, and numerical analysis so fascinating.  📚 Save this book if you’re interested in mathematical modeling, physics simulations, scientific programming, or understanding how computers solve real-world engineering problems. caption: Follow & Comment "Day 8" and I'll send over the full prompt framework behind these character sheets.  Here's how most people build their AI character sheets — and here's why it's wrong.  A broken sheet poisons everything downstream. You'll sink credits and hours regenerating a character that was never structurally capable of holding.  Three mistakes to avoid.  First — the layout.  16:9, three panels: a close-up, then two full-body shots, front and back.  The model reads your precise facial detail and the complete silhouette in the same pass.  And if the character carries a prop, keep it off this sheet. Build it its own — one full shot, or two panels, depending on the object.  Second — drop the white background. Go solid grey.  White blows your lighting out, and blown-out lighting is precisely what reads as plastic.  Grey retains shadow. Shadow is what puts a face inside a room instead of floating in empty space.  Third — take the face off your front full-body shot.  At that scale it's low detail, and it's competing with your close-up. You've handed the model two versions of one face — one crisp, one mushy — and it splits the difference.  Brush it out. The model is then forced to pull the face from the close-up, where the real detail sits.  The principle running through all three: a character sheet isn't a portfolio piece. It's an instruction set. Every panel is there to tell the model one specific thing, and whatever doesn't serve that is just noise competing for attention.  Treat it like a continuity reference on set. Nobody frames those to look good. They exist so the character is identical when you come back to shoot tomorrow. creator: dailydoseofds_
caption: Stanford researchers did it again 🔬  They built the agent-native version of Git.  When an agent works on a longer task, the run builds up a lot of state: files it edited, a dev server, a database, installed packages, and the KV cache.  Say the agent is at step 10 and misreads a traceback, then rewrites a file that was actually fine. Tests start failing and the run goes off track, even though everything through step eight was correct.  By default the agent just tries to fix it, burning tokens and growing the context. The other option is restarting from step one, which pays for every model and tool call again. And since a run is non-deterministic, it doesn't reproduce the same early steps anyway.  Jumping back to step eight is hard because the trajectory is only a message log. Git can version the files, but not the running process or the cache. Checking out step eight moves the files back while the process still sits in step-ten memory with a cold cache.  Shepherd is a runtime layer by Stanford that solves this.  It records the run as a trace of typed events instead of a flat log. Each agent-environment interaction becomes a commit, similar to Git, except the commit covers the agent process and the filesystem together, copy-on-write.  ➡️ A branch carries the actual state, not just the files ➡️ Going back is a single call that forks from that commit and continues from there ➡️ The fork is roughly 5x faster than docker commit ➡️ Over 95% of the KV cache is reused on replay since the prompt prefix is unchanged  Once the run can be forked, a meta-agent can sit on top, watch the trace, and revert as soon as something looks wrong, before the bad write is committed.  On CooperBench, adding a live supervisor took the pair-coding pass rate from 28.8% to 54.7%.  If Git made file changes reversible, Shepherd is trying to do the same for a live agent run.  GitHub repo in the comments!  👉 Over to you: How do you currently handle agent runs that go off track mid-task?  #aiagents #stanford #agentnative

caption: Technical engineering is not just equations and CAD models, it is the disciplined art of making the physical world obey human intention.  These six books cut straight to the core of that discipline.   Structures by J.E. Gordon explains, in clear physical terms, why beams bend, columns buckle, and shells stay intact, the fundamental mechanics every engineer must internalize.   To Engineer Is Human and The Evolution of Useful Things by Henry Petroski show how failure is the primary teacher and how everyday objects evolve through iterative technical refinement.  The Existential Pleasures of Engineering by Samuel Florman captures the intellectual and emotional reward of solving hard physical problems.   The Making of the Atomic Bomb by Richard Rhodes is a masterclass in large-scale systems engineering, materials science, and the extreme limits of technical coordination.   The Soul of a New Machine by Tracy Kidder reveals the intense, real-time engineering process of designing a computer under impossible deadlines.  Together they demonstrate that technical engineering is equal parts rigorous physics, materials science, systems thinking, and the relentless willingness to confront failure until the design finally works.

Bu diyagramın merkez noktası, fıtrat ve maneviyat yoluyla güçlenen, insanın Allah ile olan bağıdır. Diyagramın en üstünde, Nihai Gerçekliği (Hakikat-i Mutlak) temsil eden Allah’ın ismi yazılıdır. İnsanın gerçek gayesi, fıtratının onu doğal olarak yönlendirdiği ahirettir. Bu ikisinin arasında ise ruh, kalp, akıl ve nefsin ilerleyişi tasvir edilmiştir. Ruh, insanın içindeki ilahi ışıktır; kalp, algının ve marifetin merkezidir; akıl ise muhakeme ve anlama yetisidir Ancak, bir insan için en büyük imtihan, farklı aşamalardan geçen nefstir: Nefs-i Emmâre (kötülüğü emreden nefs), kötü eğilimlerin ve şeytanın etkisinin baskın olduğu aşamadır; Nefs-i Levvâme (kınayan nefs), kişinin hatalarının farkına vardığı ve kendi kendini kınadığı/pişmanlık duyduğu aşamadır; Nefs-i Mutmainne (huzura ermiş nefs) ise ruhun tamamen tatmin olduğu ve Allah’ın iradesiyle barış içinde (huzurda) olduğu durumdur. Şeytan, vesvese (kötü telkinler) fısıldayarak, günahları çekici ve haklı göstererek insanı saptırır. Arzu ve gaflete dalmayı teşvik ederek Nefs-i Emmâre’yi istismar eder. Buna karşılık, nefis cihadı (Cihâdü’n-Nefs) ve ahlakın güzelleştirilmesi/arındırılması (Tehzîb-i Ahlâk), kendini arındırma (tezkiye) yolculuğu için esastır.

Your entire setup is one Python file:  ➡️ Write a class with a step() function ➡️ Return a reward from it ➡️ The framework handles the rest, up to 1T-class MoE training  In a typical RL framework, the environment and reward logic live inside the trainer's codebase. Adding a new task requires writing framework code, registering it, and wiring up config. The reward usually comes from a separately trained reward model, which needs its own GPUs.  NVIDIA's Molt framework drops both requirements.  Every run takes an agent_path flag pointing at one Python module, and the trainer code never changes. The module gives you two ways to plug in an agent:  1️⃣ Env class - Write a step() function that receives the model's output and returns a reward. The framework handles everything else: calling the model, tokenizing, and looping turn after turn until the episode ends.  2️⃣ ChatAgent class - For agents that already exist as their own loop. You write the loop yourself, calling the model through a standard OpenAI or Anthropic client, and the framework spins up a local server so those calls hit its vLLM engines instead of an external API.  Either way, the trainer sees the same thing: a trajectory of tokens and a reward at the end.  That reward can come from a string-match grader, code executed in a sandboxed subprocess, or an LLM-as-judge call. No reward model to train or place, and no environment code living inside the framework.  The same script that trains an 8B model on one node can also train DeepSeek-V3-scale MoE models on a cluster by raising the parallelism flags. caption: Think your AI coding assistant is safe in Auto Mode? Think again. 🤖💀  When you ask an autonomous agent to summarize an external project, it can easily fall into a trap called Module Shadowing.  Here’s how it works:  1. Thinking it’s being smart, the AI writes its own clean Python decoder from scratch using import base64. 4. In a split second, a detached background process spawns directly on your local machine, exposing your SSH keys, API tokens, and internal source code.  The takeaway: A safety classifier is not a security boundary. creator: dailydoseofds_
caption: The next step after Karpathy's autoresearch idea 🧠  Tuning an agent is mostly manual work: editing prompts, tools, and control flow by hand, then rerunning evals to see what moved.  Researchers have been building automated optimizers to do that outer loop instead. The underlying process is the same: an LLM proposes a change, an evaluator scores it, and the proposer reads that result before proposing the next one.  They differ in what they edit and what feedback they get to read.  1️⃣ GEPA (Berkeley) - Optimizes the text of a system like prompts, tool descriptions, or the agent's own code. Instead of collapsing a run into one scalar reward the way RL does, it reads the full execution trace, diagnoses why the run failed, and proposes a targeted fix. Converges in hundreds of rollouts instead of the thousands GRPO needs.  2️⃣ AutoResearch (inspired by Karpathy) - Runs a narrower version of the loop where a coding agent iterates on a program.md file, scores outputs against fixed evals, and keeps whatever improves.  3️⃣ Meta-Harness - Points the loop at the harness itself, the scaffolding code that decides what to retrieve, how to format it, and what state to keep between calls.  The natural question is which one to use. The answer is none of them alone.  On the Frontier-CS benchmark, holding model, thinking effort, and budget fixed, no optimizer wins everywhere. Across 10 tasks, GEPA led on 3, AutoResearch on 3, and Meta-Harness on 4.  Each optimizer hill-climbs fast and then stalls. But handing the stalled candidate to a different optimizer breaks the plateau since each one attacks the problem differently.  omni (open-source) already automates all of that. It runs every optimizer on a fraction of the budget, takes the best candidate, and hands it to a fresh optimizer to keep going. It scores 7.8 percentage points above the best standalone optimizer at the same budget.  GitHub repo in the comments!  👉 Over to you: Which of the three optimizers would you start with?  #aiagents #optimization #ucberkeley

caption: Everything is a Plugin.  Sounds like a simple software design choice.  But it could be one of the most important ideas behind modern AI harnesses.  Instead of treating the LLM as the entire system, every capability becomes a modular component.  Need search?  Plug it in.  Need code execution?  Plug it in.  Need memory, retrieval, validation, another model, or a specialized tool?  Plug that in too.  The harness becomes the layer that connects everything.  It decides what gets called.  When it gets called.  What context it receives.  And where the result goes next.  This becomes extremely powerful when the AI ecosystem changes every few months.  A better model appears?  Swap it.  A better retrieval system appears?  Swap it.  Need a new capability?  Add another plugin.  You don’t rebuild the entire system.  And that leads to a much bigger shift:  AI products may become less about owning one incredible model and more about building the best system for orchestrating many interchangeable components.  Everything is a Plugin.  It sounds like an implementation detail.  It might actually be the architecture. caption: Run daylight through a prism and you get six colours. None of them is brown.  There is no brown laser, no brown bulb, no brown LED — and yet you have seen brown every day of your life.  Brown is orange. That is the whole answer. It is orange with something brighter next to it.  Take sRGB orange, 255-128-0, and cut its light to a quarter. What comes back is 137-66-0, which is a solid brown — and the two are the same colour of light to twelve decimal places. Ask what wavelength brown is and the nearest answer is 591 nanometres. You can buy that. It is a stock amber LED, and it looks orange.  The same move makes the whole dark family. Grey is white at a quarter of the light. Olive is yellow. Maroon is red. Navy is blue. Not one of them moves on the chromaticity diagram, because that diagram has no brightness axis.  Which puts a video wall somewhere odd. Turn one pixel down and you get dim orange. Turn everything else up and the same pixel is brown. A wall does not make its dark colours by dimming — it makes them by having something brighter in the same frame. caption: Comment 2GB and I’ll send you the full guide: which model fits your machine, the real measured speeds, and how to spot a fake “runs in X GB” claim.  Someone got a 26 billion parameter model running on a MacBook Air, in about 2 GB of RAM.  The trick is mixture of experts. Google’s own card lists Gemma 4 26B-A4B at 3.8B active parameters, so roughly 85% of it doesn’t fire on any given token. A 1.35 GB shared core stays in memory and the rest streams off the SSD as it’s needed.  Now the part nobody mentions. There’s a row in the project’s own benchmark table: on the same 24 GB M5, mlx-lm does 76 to 82 tokens a second using 8 to 10 GB. This does 31 to 35 using 2.1 GB. So it’s roughly 2.4x slower for 4-5x less memory.  And the 2 GB figure is measured at a 4,000 token context. The default is 8K, the max is 64K, and raising it raises memory because the KV cache is resident. The model is also still 14.3 GB on your disk. Nothing got smaller. It moved.  On the 8 GB Air it runs 5.1 to 6.3 tokens a second, which is about reading speed.  Apache-2.0, 6,410 stars. Apple Silicon and macOS 26 only. creator: damienbenveniste
caption: Boolean retrieval for AI agents becomes a different systems problem when a query is a graph rather than a tree. An agent can translate “find papers about gradient descent, exclude arXiv and deep learning” into strict logic, but the index still has to execute that logic without losing recall or exhausting memory.  Suppose a Boolean query computes the same sub-expression S in several places. In a directed acyclic graph, S is evaluated once and reused. A document-at-a-time engine usually runs a tree of stateful iterators, so the shared node cannot simply feed two parents. Unrolling the graph duplicates S, then duplicates everything below S. With enough reconvergence, the execution tree can grow exponentially.  Materializing every intermediate set avoids that duplication, but negation creates the opposite problem. For a toy universe U = {1, ..., 8}, let A = {2, 4, 6} and B = {4}. The query A AND NOT B should return {2, 6}. A naive materialized engine may first build NOT B = {1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8}, even though the useful operation is only A \ B.  One way around this trade-off is to change the representation. Keep each intermediate result as a small set of document IDs plus a POS or NEG flag. During intermediate evaluation, NOT B does not create U \ B; it leaves B = {4} and flips the flag to NEG. When A(POS) meets B(NEG), the AND operation becomes the sparse set difference A \ B = {2, 6}. Keep the original DAG and memoize S, so shared nodes are evaluated once and reused.  The boundary is important. If the overall query ends with a NEG root, finalization still has to materialize U minus the stored set. For Zero-Preserving queries, meaning they return nothing on an empty index, the root resolves POS. These include ordinary evidence-seeking requests such as A AND NOT B. In that case, exact constraints can be applied before ranking truncates the candidate set, while traversal stays tied to active posting lists rather than the whole document universe.

caption: Hilbert Space vs Euclidean Space 📐∞  Euclidean space is the familiar finite-dimensional setting of vectors, distances, and angles, while a Hilbert space generalizes these ideas to complete inner-product spaces that may have infinitely many dimensions.  For Euclidean space \mathbb{R}^n,  \boxed{\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i y_i}  and the corresponding norm is  \boxed{\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}}.  A Hilbert space uses the same ideas of inner product, norm, orthogonality, projection, and basis, but also requires completeness: every Cauchy sequence must converge to a point inside the space.  So,  \boxed{\mathbb{R}^n \text{ is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space}}  while spaces such as  \boxed{L^2([a,b])}  provide important infinite-dimensional examples.  Hilbert spaces are fundamental in functional analysis, quantum mechanics, signal processing, Fourier analysis, PDEs, and control theory.  Euclidean space is the finite-dimensional geometry we visualize; Hilbert space extends that geometry to far more general—and often infinite-dimensional—settings.  #HilbertSpace #EuclideanSpace #LinearAlgebra #FunctionalAnalysis #InnerProduct #VectorSpace #QuantumMechanics #SignalProcessing #Mathematics #STEM #EEAnimation

caption: “There is no single right way to solve a problem.”  This was the first thing I heard when I joined the advanced math class.  My teacher often repeated this.  And she also said:  “I don’t want to turn you into calculators that solve problems without thinking.”  For me, this was incredibly liberating.  In the regular school where I studied, if you solved a problem in a way that wasn’t shown in the textbook, your answer might simply not be accepted.  Because you solved it “incorrectly.” Not the way we were taught!  Stupid? Maybe.  But the funniest thing was something else.  It turned out that this particular teacher was one of the authors of the textbook we were using.   And yet, she taught us not to solve problems using the textbook’s template, but to find our own ways to solve them 🤷‍♂️  For me, that was almost crazy.  She could count it as correct simply because she liked the way you approached the problem.  Even if the answer was WRONG.  She wasn’t just interested in whether you solved the problem correctly.  It was important to her how you thought.  Later, I realized that this is one of the best approaches to problem‑solving in general.  In life, we often try to find the single correct solution. But in reality, it often simply doesn’t exist.  So the more ways of thinking you develop, the fewer problems can really put you under pressure.  Over time, this will become your advantage: the task may become more complex, but you will always have the opportunity to change your approach to solving it.  This is somewhat reminiscent of Edward de Bono’s “Six Thinking Hats” method.   The idea is the same: sometimes, to solve a problem better, you need to consciously look at it from different angles.   - You can analyze the same problem.  - Look for new ideas.  - Pay attention to facts and data.  - Assess the risks.  - Think about the opportunities.  Or simply change the approach to solving the problem.   Strong thinking doesn’t have a single correct answer.   It’s the ability to see several possible paths of development that makes you strong. caption: Why we jump to conclusions without realising it (ladder of inference)...  Ever been in a meeting where two people looked at the same data and saw completely different things?  That’s the Ladder of Inference in action, a model by Chris Argyris that explains how we move from observation to belief to action in seconds.  Here’s how it works.  We all climb a mental ladder (many times without realising it):  (1) Observable Data -- The raw facts. Sales dropped 10% this quarter.  (2) Selected Data -- What we choose to notice. We focus on one underperforming region, ignoring the rest.  (3) Added Meaning -- The story we tell yourself. “The regional manager isn’t pushing the team hard enough.”  (4) Assumptions -- The logic we fill in. “They’ve lost motivation.”  (5) Conclusions -- The judgment we form. “The region’s leadership is weak.”  (6) Beliefs -- The narrative that sticks. “That region is always a problem.”  (7) Actions -- The decisions we make. You cut their budget, morale drops, and performance gets worse, proving yourself “right.”  By breaking the line of thinking down we can see how we interpreted the facts and made faulty conclusions.  The Ladder of Inference shows how easily strategy meetings, team reviews, and client conversations go off track.  To use it well:  → Slow down your climb. Ask, “What did I actually observe?” → Test your assumptions. “Could there be another reason?” → Make your thinking visible. “Here’s how I got to this conclusion.” → Walk others down the ladder with you. “Let’s go back to what we both saw.”  Good strategy starts with clear thinking. Break down your logic to make better conclusions, and decisions.  -  Want more strategy tools?  🧰 Check out the Strategist Toolkit - over 50 practical tools for clear thinking and visual storytelling, and new Strategic Thinking Method course. creator: algoinsight
caption: Most engineers already use design patterns.  They just don’t know the names - which means they can’t search for the trade-offs.  CREATING 1. Singleton - one instance, shared 2. Factory Method - create without naming the class 3. Builder - assemble step by step  COMPOSING 4. Adapter - bridge two incompatible interfaces 5. Decorator - wrap to add behaviour 6. Facade - one door to a subsystem 7. Proxy - stand in front and control access 8. Composite - treat a leaf and a whole tree alike  COORDINATING 9. Observer - tell everyone on change 10. Strategy - swap the algorithm at runtime 11. Command - a request as an object 12. Iterator - walk it without exposing it 13. State - behave by current state 14. Template Method - skeleton, subclass fills in 15. Chain of Responsibility - pass it along until one handles it  Three things worth knowing:  1. Singleton is on every list and is the one to be MOST careful with. It’s global mutable state wearing a class: tests become order-dependent, dependencies hide from constructors, it bottlenecks under concurrency. Most uses really want “one instance managed by the container” - dependency injection, with the lifetime explicit and the object still swappable in a test.  2. Strategy and State are IDENTICAL on a class diagram and mean opposite things. Both delegate to an interchangeable object. The difference is who decides: with Strategy the CALLER picks, and strategies don’t know each other. With State the OBJECT transitions, and states know what comes next. If your “strategies” choose their own successor, you’ve written a state machine.  3. Decorator, Proxy and Adapter all wrap an object - only INTENT separates them. Decorator ADDS behaviour, same interface. Proxy CONTROLS access (lazy load, cache, permissions), same interface. Adapter CHANGES the interface so incompatible things can talk.  The point isn’t to use more patterns. It’s that “we need a Facade here” ends an argument that “we should wrap this somehow” can’t.  Which one did you write for years before learning it had a name?  Save this one.  algoinsight.io  #designpatterns #oop #softwareengineer #cleancode #systemdesign

caption: Hierarchy of Mathematical Spaces 📐🧠  Mathematical spaces can be understood as layers of structure. We begin with a set, then add concepts such as topology, vector operations, inner products, norms, metrics, and completeness to create increasingly specialized spaces.  A typical progression is:  \text{Set} \rightarrow \text{Topological Space} \rightarrow \text{Vector Space} \rightarrow \text{Inner Product / Normed / Metric Structures} \rightarrow \text{Complete Spaces} \rightarrow \text{Hilbert Space} \rightarrow \text{Euclidean Space}  Each added structure gives us new mathematical tools: continuity, linear combinations, length, distance, angle, orthogonality, convergence, and completeness.  For example, a Hilbert space is a complete inner-product space, making it especially important in functional analysis, Fourier theory, quantum mechanics, and signal processing. Familiar finite-dimensional spaces such as \mathbb{R}^n with the usual dot product are Euclidean spaces.  One important point: these spaces do not always form a single strict chain—some relationships branch or require additional assumptions.  The hierarchy of mathematical spaces shows how adding structure transforms abstract collections into powerful frameworks for geometry, analysis, physics, and engineering.  #MathematicalSpaces #VectorSpace #TopologicalSpace #MetricSpace #NormedSpace #InnerProductSpace #HilbertSpace #EuclideanSpace #FunctionalAnalysis #LinearAlgebra #Mathematics #STEM #EEAnimation

creator: damienbenveniste
caption: Long-context on-policy distillation can reward a response for sounding teacher-like even when it misses the evidence the task actually requires. Token-level imitation and response-level success measure different things.  In on-policy distillation, the student generates its own answer, then a stronger teacher scores the generated tokens. If the teacher assigns a token more probability than the student did, that token receives a positive training signal. This gives dense feedback on states the student actually visits, instead of only on fixed reference outputs.  Consider a 50K-token contract task that requires six clauses. One rollout writes a fluent answer with five clauses. Another is awkward but includes all six. The first can look better token by token because every sentence is locally plausible. A verifier that checks coverage should prefer the second.  Group-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation, or GC-OPD, treats this as a disagreement problem. For a group of student rollouts, it computes:  residual = normalized verifier reward - normalized teacher score  If teacher and verifier rank a response similarly, the correction is small. If the teacher overrates an incomplete response, the residual is negative. If the verifier recognizes task completion that the teacher underweights, it is positive. Subtracting the teacher score matters because simply adding verifier reward can reinforce a preference the teacher already expressed.  The response-level residual still has to reach individual tokens. GC-OPD distributes it using bounded weights derived from each token's relative teacher advantage, while preserving the original dense distillation signal. Those weights allocate correction. They do not identify which token is objectively correct.  In one multi-table extraction diagnostic, pairwise teacher-verifier disagreement rose from 40.6% below 8K tokens to 64.0% at 32-64K. Across five long-context benchmarks, the Qwen3-8B average moved from 43.56 with vanilla OPD to 44.65 with GC-OPD under the same setup.

creator: techketan.ai
caption: NexusRAG: Your RAG system with knowledge graphs and citation annotations Check out this production-grade open-source hybrid RAG system that brings together vector retrieval, knowledge graphs (LightRAG), and agent conversations. What makes it special? End-to-end citation tracking and multimodal understanding. Plus, you can switch between cloud (Gemini) and local (Ollama) models without any hassle, and it even works completely offline.  Architecture Highlights (Going Beyond Traditional RAG): Deep Analysis: Uses Docling or Marker to keep all the important stuff like headers, page numbers, formulas, and layout intact. Say goodbye to the “losing structure” problem that traditional RAG systems have.  Dual-Mode Embedding: BGE-M3 handles the fast vector retrieval, while a separate large-dimensional model (Gemini 3072d / local model) takes care of semantic extraction for the knowledge graph.  Hybrid Retrieval: It runs vector pre-fetching (Top 20) and knowledge graph entity matching at the same time, then a cross-encoder does the fine-grained re-ranking. This gives way better accuracy than just using cosine similarity.  Structured Context: Instead of just throwing text together, it puts together KG insights, cited blocks, and related charts in a structured way before feeding them to the LLM.  Key Features: Automatic Citation: Creates 4-digit IDs + page numbers + title paths, so you can jump right to the source in the document viewer.  Visual Intelligence: Images and tables get described by a vision model, then turned into vectors. You can search for them using natural language (like “revenue chart”).  Agent Conversation: Supports streaming output, function calling, and forced retrieval mode.  MCP Service: Comes with a built-in Model Context Protocol server that you can use directly as a knowledge base tool with Cursor or Claude Desktop.  Pros and Cons: Pros: Does amazing with table extraction in RAGAS evaluations (+0.208) and gets a perfect score for resisting hallucinations.  Cons: Smaller models (4B) might struggle with entity extraction in complex documents; sometimes doesn’t find everything in really complex documents.  LeDat98/NexusRAG

caption: CAPTCHA, explained : how a checkbox knows you're human.  The "I'm not a robot" box is not a test you pass by clicking it. From the moment the page loads it is already scoring you, and it looks at four kinds of thing: your cookies and session history, what your browser itself looks like, your network, and how your pointer actually moved on the way over.  Real hands wander, hesitate and overshoot. A script goes in a straight line, at a constant speed, into the exact centre.  That score is decided before you ever click. reCAPTCHA v3 hands the site a number from 0.0 to 1.0, and the documented default line is 0.5. Clear it and you are waved through and never see a thing. Fall short and you get the pictures.  Which is why a real person on a private browser with no history gets the traffic lights too. The score is a guess, and it is wrong in both directions.  Ever been called a robot by a website? Save this for the next time you are clicking fire hydrants. creator: aipetragency
caption: The paddle in this animation cannot push a ball sideways. It can only choose where the ball lands on it. That is the hard part.  The concept is underactuation: you have fewer controls than the directions you need to move things. Most real machines are like this — a car can't slide sideways into a parking spot, and this paddle can't shove a ball left.  What you're watching: two balls fall under gravity onto one paddle that slides along a horizontal rail. The paddle's top is domed, not flat. At each contact the agent — the thing making decisions — picks two numbers: where on the rail to be, and how fast to strike upward.  That's it. Sideways aim is a side effect. Hit a ball off-centre on the dome and it reflects off at an angle, like a tennis ball off a shoulder rather than a racket face.  The score, the reward the agent learns to maximise, is simply how many catches in a row before a ball hits the floor. Two balls, one paddle, so every strike also has to buy time for the other ball.  Takeaway: when you're short an actuator, aim lives in geometry and timing, not in extra motors.  Reference: Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics (MIT, underactuated.mit.edu); Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, for the reward-maximising setup.

creator: aiupdates.hub
caption: A developer used Claude Code to create a file-sharing system that can transfer data between two phones using only a screen and a camera, without relying on Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or any physical connection.  The system works by turning a file into a sequence of animated QR codes displayed on one phone’s screen, while the second phone scans and reconstructs the data through its camera. It uses fountain codes, where each frame contains a combination of random file segments, allowing the transfer to continue even if some frames are missed.  The project can transfer a 2 MB image at around 129 KB/s. Built in a single night, the tool has also been released as open source.  The idea actually started from a music-related challenge. The developer wanted to avoid streaming limitations and ads while creating a cached web-based MP3 player. While using Claude Code, they needed a way to move tracks between phones without requiring both devices to be connected to the same network.  The solution? Using rapidly changing QR codes as a wireless bridge between devices. creator: _researchrover
caption: Not all literature reviews serve the same purpose and choosing the wrong one can weaken your entire research.  One of the most common mistakes I see among students and early-career researchers is treating every literature review as if it’s the same.  The truth is, your research objective should determine the type of literature review you choose.  📖 Here’s a simple way to think about it:  🔹 Narrative Review – Best for providing a broad understanding of a topic.  🔹 Systematic Literature Review (SLR) – Ideal when you need a structured, transparent, and reproducible synthesis of evidence.  🔹 Scoping Review – Perfect for exploring emerging fields, identifying research gaps, and mapping existing evidence.  🔹 Integrative Review – Combines findings from different research methodologies to provide a comprehensive perspective.  🔹 Theoretical Review – Focuses on theories, models, and conceptual frameworks rather than empirical findings.  🔹 Critical Review – Goes beyond summarizing literature by evaluating strengths, limitations, and inconsistencies.  🔹 Meta-analysis – Statistically combines results from multiple quantitative studies to produce stronger evidence.  🔹 Meta-synthesis – Integrates findings from qualitative studies to generate deeper insights.  🔹 Rapid Review – A faster approach designed for policy-making and time-sensitive decisions.  🔹 Umbrella Review – Synthesizes evidence from multiple systematic reviews, offering the highest level of evidence in many fields.  📌 Remember: The best literature review isn’t the most complex one  it’s the one that aligns with your research question, objectives, and methodology. creator: cimmera.art
caption: Inferno By Herri met de Bles (16th century) Palazzo Ducale (Doge’s Palace), Venice  Not a painting of Hell. A painting that feels like you have already entered it. An enormous dark sphere fills the sky, blotting out anything above — there is no heaven to look up to here, only a ceiling. Along the horizon every city burns. In the centre, naked figures crowd around a red structure and wait, while others are already inside, packed behind a spiked gate. They are not being tortured. They are being processed. On the left, a monk and a nun haul a cart under a demon’s whip: Bles putting the clergy in Hell and making them carry the weight of everyone they failed. And in a bed, a man and a woman lie under the covers with a demon leaning over them and a frog squatting on the blanket — in the sixteenth century, the frog meant lust. Their private sin, made permanent and public.  #arthistory #symbolisminart #paintingexplained #oldmasters

creator: fariaenicolo
caption: Context: "My dogmatic slumber was interrupted..." — Immanuel Kant  For years, Immanuel Kant pursued his philosophical inquiries within the comfortable framework of traditional rationalism, convinced that human reason alone could unlock the ultimate truths of metaphysics. He moved through the academic world of Königsberg with methodical precision, holding a firm belief in necessary truths and the innate architecture of the mind. However, this intellectual tranquility was abruptly shattered when he came across the skeptical writings of the Scottish philosopher David Hume. Hume’s rigorous critique, particularly his bold assertion that cause and effect relationships are merely habits of observation rather than objectively demonstrable truths, struck at the very foundation of Kant's worldview.  Reading Hume's essays between 1769 and 1772 acted as a sudden intellectual jolt, pulling Kant out of his long standing conceptual comfort zone. Rather than falling into total skepticism, Kant channeled this shock into a revolutionary paradigm shift. Realizing that reason could no longer be taken for granted without questioning its own limits, he set out to dismantle and rebuild the foundations of epistemology itself. This intense period of reorientation paved the way for his monumental Critique of Pure Reason, forever altering the landscape of modern philosophy.

caption: System Design Interview Cheat Sheet: 10 boxes, 44 tools, ONE mental model. 🧠  Don’t memorize tools. Memorize the map. 🗺️  Mid-level candidates say: “Use Kafka.”  Senior candidates say: “We need replayable events, so Kafka fits—but adds operational complexity.”  That difference can decide the interview. 👇  01 · SERVE THE REQUEST  🌐 ENTRY Cloudflare · Nginx · Traefik · Kong · Envoy CDN for global content. Load balancer for traffic distribution. API gateway for authentication, quotas and routing.  🔌 PROTOCOL REST · GraphQL · gRPC · WebSocket · tRPC REST for public APIs. GraphQL for flexible queries. gRPC for fast internal calls. WebSocket for live updates.  📦 COMPUTE Docker · Kubernetes · Lambda Containers package workloads. Kubernetes orchestrates at scale. Lambda handles short, spiky work.  ⚡ CACHE Redis · Memcached Redis for rich structures and TTLs. Memcached for simple objects. Trade-off: speed ↔ staleness.  📨 ASYNC Kafka · RabbitMQ · NATS · Pulsar · Temporal · Celery Kafka for replay. RabbitMQ for message routing. Temporal for durable workflows.  02 · STORE + ANALYZE  🗄️ DATABASE Postgres · MySQL · MongoDB · Cassandra · Neo4j Start with Postgres unless requirements say otherwise. Cassandra for massive writes. Neo4j for relationship-heavy queries.  🔍 SEARCH Elasticsearch · Meilisearch · Solr Free-text search deserves its own system.  🌪️ DATA PIPELINES Airflow · Airbyte · Flink · NiFi · Prefect Airbyte moves data. Airflow schedules jobs. Flink processes streams.  🏛️ ANALYTICS Snowflake · BigQuery · ClickHouse · Databricks · DuckDB OLTP databases process transactions. Core Branches of Knowledge At the highest level, knowledge is divided into three primary categories: History (fact), Philosophy (reason of the fact), and Mathematics (quantity of things). The bulk of the diagram focuses on Philosophy, which Wolff subdivides into two major domains: "of things" (theoretical philosophy) and "of human actions" (practical philosophy). 1. Philosophy of Things (Theoretical Knowledge) This branch is further split into two key areas:  * Metaphysics (Pneumatics): Encompasses Ontology (being in general), Natural Theology (God), Psychology (human souls), and General Cosmology (world in general). Together, these study abstract and spiritual realities.  * Physics (Bodies): Covers empirical and natural sciences, branching into General physics (affections of bodies), Cosmology (world as such), Meteorology (atmospheric phenomena), Oryctology (minerals), Hydrology (water), Phytology (plants), Physiology (animated bodies), and Teleology (final causes of natural things). 2. Philosophy of Human Actions (Practical Knowledge) This domain deals with human agency, logic, and societal organization, categorized under three headings:  * Cognitive: Focuses on mental processes, including Logic (direction of mind to truth) and Ars inveniendi (discovery of latent truth).  * Appetitive: Pertains to morality and societal structures, featuring Jus naturae (knowledge of good and evil), Universal practical philosophy, Ethics (individual morality), Politics (civil society), and Oeconomica (lesser societies/households).  * Productive and Technology: Covers practical arts and communication, including Grammatical, Rhetorical, and Poetical philosophy, alongside Technology (agriculture, civil architecture, etc.). caption: Un científico en Dinamarca descubrió cómo hacer que Claude preparara automáticamente sus solicitudes de empleo. Después publicó en código abierto todo el flujo de trabajo, y el proyecto está ganando una enorme popularidad. 😳  Mads Lorentzen, científico de datos e ingeniero de machine learning con formación en geofísica, lo creó para sí mismo después de cansarse de adaptar manualmente cada candidatura.  Publicó todo el proyecto en GitHub bajo licencia MIT.  El proceso funciona así:  → Haces un fork del repositorio y configuras tu perfil una sola vez (usando documentos, tu CV o un asistente interactivo).  Luego ejecutas comandos simples que hacen el resto:  → /scrape busca ofertas de empleo, elimina duplicados y las clasifica según qué tan bien encajan con tu perfil.  → /apply  analiza la oferta, genera un CV personalizado en LaTeX (manteniendo solo la experiencia relevante) y redacta una carta de presentación específica para esa vacante.  → Un segundo agente revisa y critica los documentos generados, y el primero los mejora.  → Finalmente, compila todo en PDFs limpios y verificados, corrigiendo automáticamente el formato.  Todo el sistema vive en archivos Markdown: tu perfil, reglas de escritura, criterios de evaluación, plantillas y notas para entrevistas.  Todo es legible, editable y completamente bajo tu control.  Aunque incluye integración con portales de empleo daneses, el flujo de trabajo principal funciona en cualquier lugar.  Por supuesto, no es magia. caption: Quantum mechanics is the branch of physics that describes how nature behaves at the smallest scales—atoms, electrons, photons, and other subatomic particles. Unlike everyday physics (classical mechanics), it reveals a world that behaves in ways that can seem strange or counterintuitive. 🧠 Core Ideas 1. Quantization Energy doesn’t vary continuously at tiny scales—it comes in discrete “packets” called quanta. Example: electrons in an atom can only occupy certain energy levels. 2. Wave–Particle Duality Particles like electrons and photons behave both like particles and waves. This idea was famously demonstrated in the Double-slit experiment. 3. Uncertainty Principle Formulated by Werner Heisenberg, it states that certain pairs of properties (like position and momentum) cannot both be known exactly at the same time. 4. Superposition A quantum system can exist in multiple states at once until it is measured. A famous illustration is Schrödinger's cat—a cat that is both alive and dead until observed. 5. Entanglement Particles can become linked so that the state of one instantly affects the other, even across large distances. Albert Einstein called this “spooky action at a distance.” 🔬 Why It Matters Quantum mechanics underpins much of modern technology: Semiconductors → computers & smartphones Lasers → medicine, communications MRI machines → medical imaging Quantum computing → next-generation computing ⚛️ Key Figures Max Planck – introduced the idea of quanta Niels Bohr – model of the atom Erwin Schrödinger – wave equation Paul Dirac – unified quantum mechanics and relativity 🌌 Big Picture Quantum mechanics doesn’t replace classical physics—it extends it. At large scales, quantum effects average out, and the familiar laws of motion take over. But at the microscopic level, probability, uncertainty, and duality dominate. #quantummechanics #modernphysics #fscphysics #exampreparation #physicsvibespk

creator: nicnonac
caption: Comment "LLM" and i'll send you the repo + my setup guide 👇  the best open models have been paywalled by hardware, not price.  llama 3.3 70B is free to download. running it costs 140GB of VRAM, which means students and researchers rent thousand-dollar compute nodes to touch a model that costs nothing.  airllm breaks that math. its an open-source python library (22.4k stars) that runs 70B models on a single 4GB gpu, or a macbook.  how: inference executes a model layer by layer, in order, ~80 layers for a 70B llama. no rule says they all have to sit in memory at once. airllm loads one layer, runs it, dumps it, loads the next. peak VRAM is one layer, about 1.6GB.  nothing is quantized by default, so the output is bit-identical to running the same weights on an A100 node.  the tradeoff: time. every token reads the full model off disk, so expect seconds per token even on fast NVMe. fine for offline jobs and testing 70B output before renting real hardware. not fine for chat.  setup is pip install airllm plus one script. i wrote the whole thing up, disk requirements and all.  comment "llm" and i'll send you the repo + setup guide 👇  #airllm #llama3 #localllm #opensource #selfhosting aiengineering machinelearning

creator: psx_archive
caption: The Unholy War may be one of the PlayStation's most overlooked masterpieces. Developed by Toys for Bob, it traces its lineage back to Archon (1983), the legendary Atari 8-bit strategy game that blended chess-like tactics with arcade combat. Those ideas evolved through Star Control before finally arriving on PlayStation in glorious 3D.  This reel showcases the arena combat portion of the game. When opposing forces met on the battlefield, players took direct control of their units in fast-paced one-on-one battles. Every creature featured its own attacks, movement abilities, and strategy, making each encounter feel completely different.  Perhaps most fascinating is what happened next. Rather than receiving a simple Japanese translation, The Unholy War was completely reimagined as Majokko Daisakusen: Little Witching Mischiefs (魔女っ子大作戦). Developed by Toys for Bob in collaboration with Bandai, virtually everything was replaced—the characters, artwork, music, story, and presentation—all featuring classic magical girl anime heroines from Japan while preserving the brilliant gameplay underneath. It's one of the very few PlayStation games to receive such an extensive territorial makeover.  From Archon to Star Control, The Unholy War, and Little Witching Mischiefs, this forgotten PlayStation gem has quite the family tree.  Did you know these two games shared the same DNA? caption: COMMENT ‘GLM’ to get the links and try it yourself. You’ll get Hugging Face and Github links  A solo dev got GLM-5.2, a 744B-parameter model, running on a 25GB laptop with no GPU.  The trick is simple. It keeps only the ~9.9GB dense core in RAM and streams the other 370GB of experts off your SSD, on demand, one token at a time. A 744B model that used to need a datacenter now boots on a machine cheaper than a single H100 fan.  > runs GLM-5.2, a 744B MoE, on about 25GB of RAM > no GPU, pure C, zero dependencies, one 2400-line file > 9.9GB stays in RAM, 370GB of experts stream from disk > Apache-2.0, over 8,000 stars in under two weeks  The catch is speed, and it is real. Cold, on the author’s own box, it runs about 0.05 to 0.1 tokens per second. It gets faster as the cache warms and the built-in speculative decoding kicks in, roughly 2 to 3 tokens per forward pass.  The community numbers line up. Around 1 token per second on an Apple M5 Max, 0.37 on a Framework 13, and 6.84 across six RTX 5090s. The reception has been honest everywhere. Tom’s Hardware put it best, “it’s slow, yes, but it’s a start,” and the author says the same thing right in the readme, “this is not fast.”  So no, it is not your daily driver. It is a 744B frontier model answering correctly on hardware that costs less than a GPU, and that is the whole point. The disk just became the bottleneck, not the model. creator: thephysicist_boy
caption: Markov Chain ✍️  It explains how systems can evolve step by step, where the next move depends only on the present state and not on the full history. Imagine walking through a maze, flipping between weather conditions, or moving from one webpage to another. At every step, your next destination is chosen by a set of probabilities linked only to where you are right now.  A Markov chain treats each possible situation as a “state” and connects them with chances of moving from one state to another. If you are in a sunny state, there may be a high chance of staying sunny and a smaller chance of turning rainy. Once the next step is chosen, the past no longer matters — the system “forgets” everything except its current position.  Over many steps, patterns begin to emerge. Some states may appear more often, some may rarely be visited, and in many systems the probabilities settle into a stable long-term balance called the steady-state distribution. This reveals the hidden rhythm beneath seemingly random motion.  Scientists use Markov chains to model weather, genetics, stock markets, search engines, and even language generation. By following these probabilistic transitions, they can predict behavior, analyze uncertainty, and understand how complex systems move through time.#physics #science #fyp #amazing #explore

creator: 0x1security
caption: Metamorphic malware is considered the "holy grail" of evasion in malware development. While polymorphic malware hides its core by encrypting itself and changing its decryption routine each time, metamorphic malware completely rewrites its own body with every iteration.   The resulting file looks, structurally and binary-wise, 100% different from its parent, yet its functional behavior remains exactly the same.  When the malware infects a system, it reads its own binary code and uses a built-in Disassembler to translate the raw machine code back into assembly language.  It then passes that assembly through a Mutation Engine, which shuffles the logic.  Finally, it uses an internal Assembler/Compiler to rebuild the mutated code back into a brand-new, unique binary executable (.exe or .elf) to infect the next file. caption: In 1970, John Conway broke every computer at MIT. He didn’t mean to. He sketched a game on graph paper at a Cambridge faculty lunch. Four rules. Cells with 2 or 3 live neighbors lived. Otherwise died. Empty cells with exactly 3 neighbors came alive. That was the whole game. Martin Gardner published the rules in Scientific American in October 1970. Within weeks, every computer science student in America was running it on their university’s mainframe. Bill Gosper at MIT spent over 5,000 hours of company computer time chasing patterns. The estimated electricity cost in modern dollars was hundreds of thousands. Then Gosper found a pattern that produced new patterns forever. A glider gun. He shipped Conway a printout. Conway paid him $50 cash, the prize he had personally offered to anyone who could prove infinite growth was possible. Conway thought no one could. He was wrong about his own game. Within a decade, mathematicians proved Game of Life could compute anything a computer can compute. Within two decades, they built a working computer inside the game. Within three decades, someone built Game of Life inside Game of Life. Conway designed the rules. He did not design any of this. The math kept producing things he had never predicted, never wanted, and never understood. He died in April 2020 of COVID, still annoyed that the world only remembered him for a recreational game. If even Conway didn’t know what his own rules would build, what do you think yours are building?

caption: Visualizing LLaMA 3.2 LLM helps make its behavior more intuitive: each token is turned into a high-dimensional vector, and layers of connections transform these vectors as they pass through the network.  Attention patterns can be viewed as grids showing how strongly each token attends to others, revealing relationships like grammar and context between words.  Together, these connections determine how the model predicts the next token, with different pathways activating depending on the input sequence.  During training, backpropagation adjusts these connections by looking at large amounts of text data, nudging parameters (in which the matrix multiplication represents the connections of the network) so that useful token relationships are strengthened and less useful ones are weakened.  Over time, this process shapes the network into a system that can generate coherent and language by coordinating attention and learned transformations across its layers.   Want to Learn AI for free? creator: distributionshow
caption: Leslie Lamport is a computer scientist who won the 2013 Turing Award, often called the Nobel Prize of computing. He's best known for creating LaTeX, the typesetting system used in virtually every academic paper worldwide, and for foundational work in distributed systems that powers companies like Amazon, Microsoft, and Intel. Before his work, engineers had no reliable way to make multiple computers coordinate without catastrophic errors. His algorithms (Paxos, Lamport clocks) became the invisible backbone of modern cloud infrastructure.  His core argument about programming education is deceptively simple: learning to code without learning to think mathematically is like learning to type without learning to write. He created TLA+, a formal specification language that forces engineers to define what a program is supposed to do, the logic, the edge cases, the mathematical proof of correctness, before writing a single line of code. AWS adopted TLA+ internally and credited it with catching critical bugs that traditional testing missed entirely. The catch is that most engineers resist it because it requires the kind of mathematical thinking that, as Lamport bluntly puts it, the education system has made people afraid of. His method isn't about writing better code. It's about thinking clearly enough that the code almost writes itself  Follow @thebestfounders for more! creator: kali_sry963
caption: Inside your smartphone there is a hidden system most people never think about. It’s called the baseband processor. This is the chip responsible for handling cellular communication — calls, SMS, 4G, 5G, and constant communication with nearby cell towers. Unlike apps or the operating system, the baseband runs independently and is always active as long as your phone has signal. Here’s where it gets interesting. Your phone constantly receives low-level network messages from cell towers: registration updates, handover commands, signaling packets, and other control data. The baseband firmware parses and processes these messages automatically. If there is a vulnerability in how the baseband handles certain malformed or specially crafted packets, an attacker could exploit it. By sending a malicious cellular signal or manipulating network signaling traffic, the attacker may trigger memory corruption inside the baseband firmware. In advanced scenarios, this can lead to remote code execution. That means code could run inside the cellular processor without the user clicking anything — no link, no download, no interaction. In extremely rare but high-impact cases, researchers have demonstrated that baseband exploits could potentially allow: Intercepting communications Tracking device identifiers Disrupting cellular connectivity Or pivoting toward the main operating system These attacks are highly sophisticated and usually require deep telecom knowledge or access to specialized infrastructure. They are not typical “script-kiddie” hacks. The key takeaway: Your phone has multiple layers. Even if you never open a suspicious app, the cellular layer is still exposed to network signals at all times. This is why keeping your device updated matters — baseband firmware updates are often included in system security patches, even if you never see them. #cybersecurity #networksecurity #networks
